name: A Tale of Two Middle Classes
description:
How has the transformation of the Indian economy over the 21st century shaped the lives of ordinary Indians?  
This talk traces the evolution of India’s middle classes through data from the India Human Development Survey, a study that repeatedly interviewed more than 40,000 households between 2004 and 2024. Grounded in these lived experiences, the talk examines the size and origins of both the upper and lower middle classes, exploring their lifestyles and aspirations as they navigate a changing, and at times uncertain, economy.

name: How Far a Note Travels: The Nadhaswaram and a Music Built for Distance
description:
The nadhaswaram is a mangala vadyam (auspicious instrument) is not merely an accompaniment, but rather an active part of what makes an occasion sacred. This session aims to help listeners hear gamaka, the sliding ornamentation that gives a raga its identity, most audible on the nadhaswaram’s fretless pipe. The instrument’s global cousins are featured, from the Turkish zurna to the Chinese suona. The session closes with Sheikh Chinna Moulana, the Muslim vidwan from a three-century lineage who became Asthana Vidwan at Srirangam and Tirupati. 
The nadhaswaram answers the challenge of filling a temple town with music, outdoors, with no electricity, through brute acoustic engineering: a two-and-a-half-foot cone of hardwood with a double reed, played with circular breathing so the sound never stops. Paired with the tavil, a drum of comparable force, the periya melam (big ensemble) was built to carry across a moving procession, over crowds in open air, for hours. The families who played it, Isai Vellalar, were classified under the Sudra varna, and considered ritually polluting, even as no temple ceremony could proceed without their music. When the microphone arrived in the mid-twentieth century, the acoustic problem the instrument was built to solve simply disappeared. T.N. Rajarathnam Pillai, the tradition’s greatest player, responded by redesigning it: a longer body, a lower pitch, tone built for carrying power. Discover its history, tradition and resonant sound this evening, 
Recordings are drawn from the Archive of Indian Music, Smithsonian Folkways and other archival sources, with acknowledgement from the stage.

name: It’s Time to Put Nutrition First
description:
Sylvia Karpagam discusses her book Meat of the Matter, challenging prejudices and misconceptions around food in India. Is malnutrition in India simply a policy failure, or are there structural conditions which make it so? 
The conversation explores the political, social, and economic contexts surrounding food practices across the country, arguing that malnutrition is structural, not incidental. Beyond failing policies and poorly implemented programmes, Karpagam highlights the role discrimination plays at every level, implicating researchers, academicians, bureaucrats, elected representatives, and the media in perpetuating stereotypical narratives that need to be broken. Small improvements in nutritional indicators, she argues, cannot be read as “successes,” since those left behind face outcomes that are significant, and often irreversible.

name: The Siachen Glacier - Managing Mountains and War
description:
Inside the world’s highest, harshest battlefield, this talk covers not only the mountains but the war, politics, financial cost, and human toll of the ongoing conflict in Siachen. Here, India, Pakistan, and China have been engaged in hostilities for decades. The talk includes over 180 photographs documenting the Siachen Glacier and the people involved. 
Drawing on visits to the region since 1980, including reaching Karakoram Pass, Col Italia, and Indira Col, the three northernmost points of India, the talk traces the Indian Army’s role in the glacier, the young soldiers who serve there, and the sacrifices they make. It considers the challenges civilian expeditions face on the glacier, questions of leadership, and a proposal for a “Siachen Peace Park” to end the conflict. Though a ceasefire holds today, soldiers continue to endure the glacier’s harsh conditions. 
In collaboration with: 
The Himalayan Club
Founded in 1928, the Himalayan Club is one of the earliest mountaineering clubs established in the subcontinent, with a presence across India and abroad. Its objectives extend beyond climbing to publications, awards, lectures, social activities, sponsorships, and mountain film festivals. First published in 1928, The Himalayan Journal has earned worldwide recognition as the most reliable reference on the Himalaya, Karakoram, and Hindukush. Members include some of the most decorated mountaineers and explorers in India and abroad. The club will soon celebrate its centenary year!

name: Beyond ‘I like It’
description:
What makes an artwork meaningful? This talk journeys across cultures, time periods, and artistic mediums to discover how artworks speak in different visual languages, leaving audiences with simple tools to look at the world around with greater curiosity, confidence, and attention. 
The aim of the session is to cultivate visual literacy; the ability to observe carefully, recognize that images are constructed rather than neutral, and appreciate how meaning emerges through the interplay of form, material, history, culture, and the viewer’s own experience. Across cave paintings, temple sculpture, photography, contemporary installations, and even the images encountered every day, the question thus transforms from, “What does this artwork mean?” to, “How is meaning being made here?”

name: Non-Aligned Modernism
description:
What does it mean to build a nation’s identity from scratch? This lecture traces the life of Aditya Prakash, one of India’s first Modernist architects. His son, Vikramaditya Prakash, explores his body of work that reflects the idea of non-aligned modernism — a third way of building a modern, internationalist identity of a newly independent nation, resisting allegiance to either capitalist or communist blocs. 
Born in 1924 in colonial India, Aditya Prakash trained in London before joining the Chandigarh Capital office as a junior architect under Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret. Over the following decades, he designed nearly 100 buildings and urban plans, while also working as an artist, sculptor, furniture designer, and theatre actor. For him, architecture, sculpture, and performance were never separate disciplines, but expressions of a single question: how to live fully while keeping the interests of the poorest at heart. He called this his “continuous line” — the philosophical thread that ran through everything he made.

name: Beyond Digitisation
description:
This lecture explores the study of Indic manuscripts, examining what it takes to turn a digitised artefact into a source for reconstructing South Asia’s religious, philosophical, and cultural history. Digital images can preserve a manuscript, but can they ever truly read it? 
Drawing on case studies from Nepal, India, China, and Japan, as well as discoveries from Buddhist, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, and Jaina manuscript traditions, the lecture demonstrates how the careful study of manuscripts, through descriptive cataloguing, palaeographical and codicological analysis, and critical text editing, has transformed our understanding of South Asia’s intellectual past. It highlights the crucial role of manuscript colophons, textual criticism, and scholarly editing in recovering lost works, tracing the transmission of ideas, and revealing historical networks that would otherwise remain invisible. Over the past half-century, large-scale preservation initiatives, including the Nepal-German Manuscript Preservation and Cataloguing Projects and India’s National Mission for Manuscripts and Gyan Bharatam, have safeguarded millions of manuscript folios through microfilming and digitisation. The lecture argues that the future of Indic manuscript studies lies not in digitisation alone, but in integrating digital humanities with rigorous cataloguing, critical editing, and international scholarly collaboration.  
The session is preceded by a talk by Prof. K Ramasubramanian on “The Elusive Ratio and the Advent of Calculus in India” at 5pm.

name: Re-Garde
description:
Re-Garde is a contemporary dance piece moving between opposing pairs: youth and old age, control and release. As the choreographers describe it, the piece traces how our way of observing the world, people, art, conflict, each other, transforms from childhood to adulthood, shaped by the societies and environments we inhabit. 
Exploring the sense of sight, the performance follows two performers as mirrors of each other’s projections, ready to give, lose, provoke and be provoked; crossing the delicate boundaries that separate them, suspended between gesture and poetry. What does it mean to look at the world clear-sighted, unconditioned, free?

name: Kuchipudi Yakshaganam
description:
At 85 years of age, Guru Sri Pasumarthi Rattaiah Sarma Garu remains one of the last living custodians of the Kuchipudi Yakshagana tradition, a dance-drama format that seamlessly integrates dance, music, abhinaya, dialogue, and the singing of padyams by the performer. Kuchipudi dancer Aishwarya Meenakshi presents this evening, offering a chance to witness dharavus from this near-forgotten repertoire. 
Distinct from the solo recital format commonly seen today, Kuchipudi Yakshaganam is a collaborative and immersive performance practice accompanied by a live orchestra, preserving the form’s historic character as a total theatre tradition. This presentation serves as an act of cultural preservation and transmission. It is a rare opportunity to encounter, celebrate, and document a vital chapter in the history of Kuchipudi directly from one of its most distinguished torchbearers.

name: The Pursuit of Truth: The Kosambi Legacy
description:
From Buddhist philosophy and social reform to mathematics and Sanskrit literature, the Kosambis challenged inherited orthodoxies across disciplines, geographies, and public movements. This lecture explores the extraordinary intellectual legacy of Dharmanand and D.D. Kosambi, father and son, two restless twentieth-century Indian minds, drawing on Ram Ramaswamy’s double biography of the pair. 
What does it take to bridge knowledge and social responsibility? D.D. Kosambi was a mathematician, historian, numismatist, and Marxist thinker; his father, Dharmanand Kosambi, was a Buddhist scholar and social reformer whose life shaped his son’s radical curiosity. Together, their work shows that ideas do not exist in isolation, and that rigorous thinking can be a powerful tool for understanding and changing the world.

name: Hoovyaru Belasidare | Who Grew the Flowers?
description:
42 minutes | Kannada with English subtitles | 2026 | India 



Hoovyaru Belasidare reimagines ideas of femininity and freedom. How do working-class women create space for their own voices in the city? How does a varied group of sex workers find common ground and a shared language for their creativity?
Sex workers have been seen as criminals, victims, survivors, and even activists, but rarely as artists and creators. This film follows the journey of Sadhana Mahila Sangha members as they tell their own stories through art. Starting with their 2014 Kannada theatre production, Hasivu Kanasu (Hunger Dreams), Sadhana members explore folk music, poetry, theatre, shadow puppetry, and film. Along the way, they examine their childhood memories, experiences of caste, encounters with police violence, friendships, and activism, offering a glimpse into their relationship with the changing city. 
Directed by Varun Kurtkoti, Hoovyaru Belasidare was produced collaboratively with Deepak Srinivasan, Gowri Vijayakumar, and the Sadhana Mahila Sangha team. The screening will be followed by a bilingual discussion in both Kannada and English, with the team behind the film.

name: Playful Body
description:
Centred on partnering, play, and humour, in this workshop participants will explore how to observe, listen and respond to the bodies all around.  
The class opens with floor work rooted in the cranio-sacral connection and the body’s spiral, moving instinctively and fluidly. Participants explore coordination and movement quality before the work evolves into partnering: exploring gravity, counterweight, off-axis balance and sensory listening through touch. It is a practice built on trust, joy and calculated risk; balancing between falling and rising, letting gravity move through the body. 
The session is led by Maxime Freixas and Francesco Colaleo, both pedagogues trained at the National Dance Centre of Lyon. They have taught across France, Italy, Poland, China and beyond, and created Falling Superstars for CODARTS’ Dance Teacher Bachelor programme in 2024.  
Please Note: The workshop is intended for Intermediate level practitioners. Though open to all ages, participants are expected to be in good physical health with no particular physical fragilities. The session has a limited capacity of 20 participants.

name: Antarnaad
description:
The call of the soul can be heard this evening. 
Rakshit Kulkarni’s recital features two Hindustani rāgas, presented in their traditional depth and grandeur. This is followed by a selection of rare Haridasa compositions in the second half of the concert. He is accompanied by Mihir Kalyanpur on tabla and Anjana Hegde on harmonium. 
The Haridasa tradition began in Karnataka centuries ago, blossoming from the Dvaita philosophy of Madhvacharya. Saint-composers like Purandara Dasa and Kanaka Dasa wrote devotional songs in Kannada, making sacred philosophy accessible to ordinary people. These compositions were originally sung in the Carnatic style, but over time, particularly in North Karnataka, Hindustani music began to shape how Haridasa songs were rendered. Vocalists like Bhimsen Joshi carried this crossover forward, and it continues today. This recital brings together both traditions, presenting Haridasa compositions through a Hindustani lens.
